headings: ### Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over: your three paragraphs

rows.label: Your boundary paragraph (in)
rows.article: Here's where I want to clearly depart from the new-age wizdumb

source.quote: Here's where I want to clearly depart from the new-age wizdumb that all your problems are self-created: Somebody may really have crossed a boundary and still have hit something old in you. You felt your stomach tighten up, and that somehow elevated the boundary crossing to “They're evil.” But you can defer that judgement for when you're in your happy place.

rows.note: Word for word, with one fix: a double space in "Just  because". Alone 100% Human (121).

rows.label: Your PGQ-001, first paragraph (in)
rows.article: Feelings about yourself work the same way.

source.quote: Preserve the distinction between a thought/sensation/attraction/aversion being real as an experience and the conclusion drawn from it. Separate experience, interpretation, and chosen action. Do not let the therapist, body, or strongest feeling of the hour decide which transient state is the person's "real" identity. Do not steer sexuality, orientation, or gender identity in either direction, and do not dismiss genuine identity-relevant experience merely because it is confusing, unwanted, or stigmatized.

rows.note: Alone 100% Human (148); your check of the two together, Human, high.

rows.label: Your PGQ-001, second paragraph (in)
rows.article: The opposite extreme of our pendulum

source.quote: The opposite mistake matters too. Don’t dismiss your own genuine attraction, orientation, gender identity, or another meaningful part of your experience as “just intrusive” or “not the real you” merely because it is unwanted, stigmatized, confusing, or conflicts with personal, family, community, or religious expectations. You do not have to force a conclusion in either direction. Separate the experience itself from the meaning you are giving it and from the urge to get certainty right now, and let repeated real-life patterns show you more over time.

rows.note: Alone 100% Human (76). Your Body Might Need Some Love First with all three: 100% Human (2,142). The h1: 97% Human, with the one AI segment in the Also Look Outward run below.
notes: Below it, Also Look Outward opens with "Once you're in that happy place", which now points back past your two new paragraphs and the heading to "your happy place". Leave it, or "Once you're in your happy place"?

headings: ### Start With Whatever Showed Up: PGQ-004

rows.label: PGQ-004, first paragraph (in)
rows.article: Anxiety deserves the same kind of listening.

source.quote: Anxiety deserves the same respect without becoming an oracle. It may be warning about overload, humiliation, danger, uncertainty, or a boundary. In ordinary-life decisions, hear the alarm, ask what it is trying to protect, and compare its prediction with evidence and what actually happens over time. But do not turn that into permission to push past a protector’s no to deeper processing or altered-state work, or past hesitation about touch or sex. Consent and immediate safety come first, and possible medical red flags get checked before they become psychological experiments. Listening to a protector is not the same as letting it drive; questioning a prediction is not the same as overriding a no.

Preserve the distinction between protective intent and predictive accuracy. Anxiety may warn about overload, humiliation, uncertainty, danger, or a boundary, but it does not automatically establish the feared conclusion. Listening is not the same as obeying, and testing a prediction never overrides consent or a protector's no to touch, sex, deeper processing, or altered-state work.

headings: ## Your Body Might Need Some Love First: the r4 pleasantness paragraphs (not in)

rows.label: Pleasantness P1
rows.text: Whatever you try from that map, I wouldn't go by how pleasant a session felt to tell whether it was good for you. This kind of work can bring up grief and fear, and sometimes hard dreams, or stuff you'd rather never have met. A session can also be really intense and get you nowhere. Even staying present the whole time doesn't tell you enough by itself. It's a bit like the gym, where sore and injured can feel pretty similar that evening, and it's the next few days that tell you which one it was.
rows.after: When your nervous system is flooded

source.quote: Do not use pleasantness as the only safety meter either. Learning often includes grief, fear, frustration, difficult dreams, or material you would rather not meet. Difficulty by itself is not harm, just as intensity by itself is not progress. But “I stayed oriented” is not enough by itself either. Ask four things: could you stop and return, do you actually want to go back toward it, did it feel difficult-but-workable rather than simply too much or unwanted, and how did you recover afterward in sleep and ordinary functioning?

notes: Between the paragraph before and this one, the article has your embedded post "Somatic Therapy Modalities Map & Free Intro Sessions!"

rows.label: Pleasantness P2
rows.text: So how were the next few days? How did you sleep, and could you get through your day okay? Do you want to go back toward what came up, or is some part of you saying no? (And could you have stopped and come back to the room, if you'd needed to? If not, I'd keep my eyes open next time, before any imagery.) If you honestly can't tell yet, I wouldn't rush to call it healing or harm. I'd just make the next one a bit easier, one change at a time, so you learn what made the difference. If you're getting worse, though, change several things at once, and have someone steady with you.

source.quote: If those answers are not known yet, do not rush to classify the experience as healing or harmful. Ask how it landed and how you have been since. Then scaffold the challenge. When you are calibrating, changing one thing at a time can teach you what matters; if distress is climbing, change several things at once. Try shorter duration, less depth or imagery, better timing, more symbolic or indirect representation, eyes open or stronger external anchors, less isolation, and more support. Restore challenge gradually only when you want to continue and recovery supports it. This is not throwing yourself into a cauldron to toughen up; it is finding the edge where you can actually learn.

Use an eyes-open, present-focused version when imagery pulls you away from the room, time, or body you are actually in. If a session leaves you less able to function, more compulsive, or less oriented to the present, shorten it and bring in grounded support rather than trying to win a contest with your own nervous system.

rows.note: Alone 100% Human (122), on the second try.

rows.label: Pleasantness P3
rows.text: Bring the challenge back gradually, and only when you want to and you're recovering well. If you're not sure yet whether you want to, you can wait. Some people try to toughen themselves up in a cauldron, but what you're looking for is the edge where you can actually learn. Those dreams and images that come up can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. They aren't evidence that what you saw in them happened, though, and shouldn't be used to confirm a memory or rebuild one. Or to suggest one.

source.quote: Dreams and imagery can be useful material about what feels important, frightening, missing, or needed now. They are not evidence that the pictured event happened historically. Do not use them to confirm, suggest, or reconstruct a memory.

rows.note: Alone 100% Human (107). With all three in, the h2 read 92% Human, and the AI segment was the Also Look Outward run below, not these.

headings: ### Also Look Outward: the run Pangram flagged, and the isolation group after it

rows.label: In the article
rows.article: If a relationship keeps making you feel less safe
rows.flag: But if they've actually hurt or threatened you, even once, old stuff or not, get safe first, which is not a small thing at all, I know.
rows.note: The flagged run starts at this sentence.

rows.label: In the article
rows.article: If you really did hurt them, repair it.
rows.flag: If you really did hurt them, repair it.

rows.label: In the article
rows.flag: You can mean the apology. Then notice what happens next. Are you sorry for what you did, or are you starting to take back the complaint too because they're still upset? Maybe your first explanation sucked. Try again. 😅 But if you've said what you mean and said no, you can't guarantee they'll understand it. Guilt may keep shouting at you. That doesn't tell you the whole conflict was yours, and it doesn't prove they're manipulating you.
rows.note: From the September lane. I tried two fixes here; each passed alone and neither cleared the h2, so this is the original.

rows.label: C1, PGQ-002 (in)
rows.article: Then there are people you're just getting to know.
rows.flag: Then there are people you're just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test.

rows.label: Isolation P1, third try
rows.text: Maybe part of what your little one went through was being alone with it. Then reaching toward people can be part of this work too, and you can call that reparenting if you like the word. Some people figure, "I'll get myself sorted out first, and then I'll be fit company for anybody." I don't think a decent parent would ask that of a lonely kid. So sometimes the grown-up thing to do is just to text someone first.
rows.after: Then there are people you're just getting to know.

source.quote: If isolation itself is part of the wound, reaching toward people may be one way the adult side provides care. If inner-child language already feels natural to you, you might call that reparenting in action. If it does not, there is no need to label it that way. A decent parent would not tell a lonely child to become perfectly self-sufficient before seeing friends; sometimes the adult move is making the call, arranging the visit, asking the social worker, or helping yourself walk into a room where people share something real.

rows.note: Alone 100% AI, three tries this turn.

rows.label: C2, PGQ-003
rows.text: And reaching out doesn't mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn't fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller things you tell them, and how they take it when you say no. But if a relationship is getting deep and you're still keeping up a fake normal, happy version of yourself to hold onto it, I'd either bring more of the truth in, carefully, or let it be less deep for now. (If telling could put you in real danger, like violence, or being outed where that isn't safe, protect yourself first.) And when someone finally accepts you, it can feel amazing. It still doesn't prove you're meant for each other, or that they've earned your trust yet.

source.quote: privacy is not fakery; total disclosure is not required. Let people earn deeper access through demonstrated handling of smaller truths, boundaries, and vulnerability.

rows.note: Alone 100% Human (130), with "reaching out" and "you're meant for each other" from a cold read and a grounding.

rows.label: Isolation P2, third try
rows.text: I'd look for more than one place to belong, too. One partner or one therapist can't be all of it, and if they're busy or gone, you'd be left with nobody. Keep the good people you've got, and then maybe add a spiritual community that fits you, or a class you keep showing up to. Not every one of them has to click. But if a group makes you feel more wanted than you've ever felt, and then someone there starts saying your old friends are holding you back, I'd let the Protector handle that one, and keep your other people, even if it means not going back.

source.quote: Look for more than one door: trusted people you already know, reciprocal friendships where possible, peer-support groups, a church, sangha, Unitarian or other spiritual community if that genuinely fits you, a book club, hiking or foraging group, class, volunteer project, professional help, or practical services. Add routes alongside the safe supports you already have rather than treating diversification as a reason to drop somebody good. You do not need every door to open. A network of several imperfect supports is usually sturdier than making one partner, friend, therapist, group, spiritual authority, service, or this app the only place you can belong.

Use the Protector here too. A community is not automatically good because it offers belonging. High-control groups, exploitative authorities, and unsafe or abusive relationships should not be reinforced as “support.”

rows.note: Alone 100% AI, three tries this turn.

headings: # Before You Try to Go Deep: the r4 depth paragraphs (not in)

rows.label: Depth P1, third try
rows.text: Your little one will still be there later. Some people want out of the whole inner-child idea, though ("this just isn't me"), and that's a different thing. If that's you, I wouldn't keep sneaking it back in through some "gentler" version, or start calling the dishes reparenting. Looking after yourself and keeping yourself safe can happen in whatever words feel like yours. Same with figuring out where you're headed, and getting support from people.
rows.after: How much of the grown-up you is actually here right now?

source.quote: That means turning the depth down, not throwing the relationship away—unless you simply do not want to use the inner-child frame. A no to the frame is not a pacing problem to solve. If you do not want inner-child work, stop using that language and do not keep trying to sneak it back in through “gentler” exercises or by renaming ordinary tasks as reparenting. Care, protection, guidance, and human support can continue in whatever language actually fits you.

rows.note: Alone 100% AI, three tries this turn.

rows.label: Depth P2, third try
rows.text: If you do want it, and it's just too much at this depth, some people try one technique after another, thinking, "I just have to push through this." I'd go shallower instead. If going inward keeps making it worse, or you're not sure you could stop and come back, I'd put the inward stuff down and come back out to the room. Once you're steadier, there's a harm-reduction saying for this: start low and go slow. Low might be doing one protective thing out in your life, or calling someone who's good for you. Or a short hello to your little one with your eyes open.

source.quote: If you do want the relationship but a particular depth is too much, preserve the relationship by changing the dose. If you cannot reliably stop, return, stay oriented, or inward attention itself is making things worse, stop the inner exercise and come outward first. Do not test another inward technique just to prove you can tolerate something. Once you are steadier, the next gentlest step might be an ordinary protective action, real human support, or a brief eyes-open acknowledgment before imagery or deeper dialogue.

rows.note: Alone 100% AI, three tries this turn.

rows.label: Depth P3
rows.text: A full pause from your little one is the last thing I'd reach for, but sometimes you need one, for safety or because nothing smaller is working. (Looking after yourself, and seeing the people who are good for you, can keep going.) I'd write down why. Then the last level you could still handle, and what would have to change before you'd go back. Some people keep taking little peeks during a pause, just a quick hello, just a bit of imagery. I'd wait. When that change is there and you want to come back, start at that last level you could handle, or lower.

source.quote: A complete tolerance pause is a last resort, and a safety problem can require a pause whether or not you want one. In that case, make the pause specific: what made it necessary, what level was last genuinely workable, and what observable change—plus your own agreement—would make a gentle return reasonable. While the pause is still active, do not keep testing gentler child-facing versions such as witnessing, imagery, or symbolic contact. Wait for the return condition instead. When you return, start at or below that last workable level rather than jumping back to where you left off. If a difficult experience still needs a check-in about how it landed or your system is still telling you to step down, settle that before trying to step back up. Changing the dose does not mean the relationship has failed, and this approach does not override your choice about whether to use inner-child framing at all.

rows.note: Alone 100% Human (109), on the second try.
